plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 6: An Overview of Organic Reactions
plan.contextChunk: This figure comprises four reaction energy diagrams arranged in a two-by-two grid and labeled (a), (b), (c) and (d) at their upper left corners. Each panel carries a tall vertical arrow at its left shaded from cream to orange and labeled Energy, a pale blue plotting field, and beneath it a horizontal axis labeled Reaction progress ending in a magenta arrow pointing right; no numbers appear on either axis. Within every field a smooth magenta curve runs from a flat reactant level, over a single rounded maximum, and down to a flat product level. Horizontal dashed lines extend from the reactant level, the top of the maximum, and the product level, and double-headed vertical arrows between those dashed lines are labeled delta G with a double dagger for the barrier height and delta G degree for the overall change. Panel (a) pairs a low barrier with a product level well below the reactants. Panel (b) shows a tall barrier above the same downhill step, its drop to product smaller. Panel (c) has only a shallow hump and ends barely above the reactant level. Panel (d) combines a very tall barrier with a product level clearly above the reactants. Because axes and curve shape stay fixed across the grid, the panels isolate two independently varying quantities: barrier height, and whether products sit above or below reactants. The set establishes that every reaction has its own energy profile.

interactionPlan.concept: A reaction's rate is set by its activation barrier (ΔG‡) while its thermodynamic favorability is set by the product–reactant energy difference (ΔG°), and these two quantities vary independently to produce the four distinct reaction profiles shown in the textbook's 2×2 grid.
elements: 2×2 grid of four panels shown in 'all four' view, each labeled (a), (b), (c), or (d) at its upper left
single enlarged panel shown in 'single profile' view, carrying the matching (a)–(d) label
vertical Energy axis arrow per panel, cream-to-orange gradient, labeled 'Energy'
horizontal axis per panel: 'Reaction progress' magenta text with the magenta arrowhead placed fully to the right of the text (or directly below it) so arrow and text never overlap
pale blue plotting field per panel, no numeric ticks on either axis
smooth magenta energy curve per panel: flat reactant plateau, single rounded maximum, flat product plateau
short horizontal dashed reference segment at the reactant energy level, near the left plateau only
short horizontal dashed reference segment at the transition-state (maximum) level, near the peak only
short horizontal dashed reference segment at the product energy level, near the right plateau only
double-headed vertical arrow between the reactant and maximum dashed segments, labeled ΔG‡
double-headed vertical arrow between the reactant and product dashed segments, labeled ΔG°, positioned near the middle of the curve (not at the far right edge)

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: The four textbook panels are simply the four combinations of two independent choices — barrier height (rate) and product energy (favorability) — visible simultaneously
Clicking one of the four grid panels isolates that profile so its ΔG‡ and ΔG° annotations can be read closely without the other three competing for attention

interactions.label: Reaction profile
interactions.teaches: Each named profile is just a combination of two independent choices — low vs. high barrier (rate) and products below vs. above reactants (favorability) — so rate and thermodynamics need not go together

interactions.label: Activation barrier ΔG‡
interactions.teaches: Raising the barrier slows the reaction but leaves ΔG° unchanged — the hump grows while reactant and product levels stay put

interactions.label: Product energy (ΔG°)
interactions.teaches: Moving the product level above or below the reactant level flips the reaction between endergonic and exergonic without changing the barrier height

demo_steps.title: The full 2×2 grid
demo_steps.narration: The default view reproduces the textbook's four panels simultaneously: barrier height (fast vs. slow) and product energy (exergonic vs. endergonic) vary independently, giving all four combinations.

demo_steps.title: Fast exergonic
demo_steps.narration: Panel (a) enlarged: a low barrier means the reaction is fast, and products sit well below reactants so ΔG° is negative — both fast and favorable.

demo_steps.title: Slow exergonic
demo_steps.narration: Panel (b): the products are still downhill, but the tall barrier makes the reaction slow — thermodynamic favorability does not guarantee speed.

demo_steps.title: Fast endergonic
demo_steps.narration: Panel (c): a shallow hump makes it fast, but products end slightly above reactants, so ΔG° is positive — a fast reaction can still be unfavorable.

demo_steps.title: Slow endergonic
demo_steps.narration: Panel (d): a very tall barrier plus products above reactants — slow and unfavorable. Now drag the two sliders yourself and watch the profile morph continuously between all four types.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: ΔG‡ (kinetics) and ΔG° (thermodynamics) are independent: any barrier height can pair with any product energy, which is why 'fast' and 'favorable' are separate questions about a reaction.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Default view is a 2×2 grid of four equal panels labeled (a) top-left, (b) top-right, (c) bottom-left, (d) bottom-right, exactly reproducing the textbook layout; 'Single profile' view replaces the grid with one enlarged panel (same styling) plus the sliders. Every panel: pale blue field, cream-to-orange vertical 'Energy' arrow at left, and a horizontal axis below whose magenta 'Reaction progress' text must sit clear of the magenta arrowhead — put the arrowhead entirely to the right of the text or directly beneath it, never overlapping the glyphs. No numeric ticks anywhere. The magenta curve is a smooth single-humped profile with flat reactant and product plateaus. Dashed reference lines are SHORT local segments only: a brief segment near the reactant plateau at the left, one near the peak, one near the product plateau at the right — each just long enough to anchor its arrow, never spanning most of the field width. The ΔG‡ double-arrow spans reactant to peak segment near the rising slope; the ΔG° double-arrow spans reactant to product segment positioned near the MIDDLE of the curve (roughly above the hump's descending region), matching source panels a/b — do not push it to the far right edge. In single view, selecting a profile type snaps the sliders to that panel's canonical values and shows the matching (a)–(d) label; dragging either slider redraws the curve smoothly and repositions the dashed segments and arrows live, keeping the peak clearly above both endpoints at all settings.

authoredContext:
Not all energy diagrams are like that shown for the reaction of ethylene and HBr. Each reaction has its own energy profile. Some reactions are fast (small ΔG‡) and some are slow (large ΔG‡); some have a negative ΔG°, and some have a positive ΔG°. The figure illustrates some different possibilities.

Some hypothetical energy diagrams: (a) a fast exergonic reaction (low ΔG‡, negative ΔG°); (b) a slow exergonic reaction (high ΔG‡, negative ΔG°); (c) a fast endergonic reaction (small ΔG‡, small positive ΔG°); (d) a slow endergonic reaction (high ΔG‡, positive ΔG°).

Four energy diagrams for different reactions with different values of delta G naught show different magnitudes of activation barrier.
